# 1: Project Overview

The aim for my project is to investigate what factors contribute to the success of video games, and i will be focusing on characteristics like genre platform, release  year,sales performance, etc.i want to look through a lot of variables to which ones perform better and how it can changed over time. My guess is that game success is influenced by genre, platform and some combinations achieving higher sales than others.

# 2: Data Sources


## 2.1 Summary of sources

```{r source-summary, echo=FALSE}
sources <- tribble(
  ~Source,            ~Producer,          ~Format,  ~Coverage,          ~Using,
  "Video Game Sales with Ratings",    "VGChartz / Metacritic; Kaggle",   "CSV",  "Multiple platforms, 1980–2016",   "Yes",
  "Steam Store Games",    "Steam Store / SteamSpy; Kaggle",   "CSV",  "PC games on Steam, collected in 2019",   "yes",
 "Essential Facts 2026", "Entertainment Software Association",  "Web report",   "United States, 2026",   "No"
)

knitr::kable(sources)
```

## 2.2.1: Video Game Sales with Ratings

**Producer and authority.** 
The dataset was compiled by Rush kirubi. Using video game sales information from VGChartz and review scores from Metacritic. it was published on kaggle for public use and analysis.I could not find evidence that it was produced under a specific research grant or government mandate.

**Original Dataset Purpose.**
The dataset was created to add video game sales  with critic and user ratings and other information. The creator suggested using the data for things like machine learning and data visualization. this will be relevant to my project because I want to find out which factors,like genre, platform, release year, and ratings, are associated with video game success.

**Collection method.** The data was collected through web scraping. the sale information was from VGChartz, and ratings and critic part was from metacritic

**Coverage and resolution.** 
The dataset contains about 16,719 records and contains video games released between 1980 and 2016 on multiple gaming platforms. Each row represents a game on a particular platform. Sales are in millions of units, with separate columns for North America, Europe, Japan, other regions, and global sales.

**Licence.** 
it shows lincense as unknown on the kaggle website.I could not confirm a specific licence granting permission to redistribute the data.

**Access.** 
The dataset is available on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/rush4ratio/video-game-sales-with-ratings/data. It can be downloaded as a CSV file, although a Kaggle account may be required. Another researcher could retrieve it from the same page.

**Known problems.** 
 One limitation i noticed is missing information, mainly for critic scores, user scores, and ESRB ratings. According to the dataset description, only approximately 6,900 records have complete observations. Metacritic does not cover every gaming platform, which is why there are missing values. The dataset also contains mostly older games(ends in 2016) and may not accurately represent the current video game industry. Finally, the sales figures are really close estimates and not actual verified transactions.

```{r source-1-load}
raw_1 <- read_csv("data/raw/Video_Games_Sales_as_at_22_Dec_2016.csv")
glimpse(raw_1) |> select(1:6) 
```


The output showed info of dataset like number of rows and column. And all column titles with with their data type(chr,dbl, etc) and a few examples of them. And under that was first 6 columns of dataset and first 10 rows of the dataset

## 2.2.2 Steam Store Games

**Producer and authority.** The dataset was put together by Nik Davis. He used information from the Steam Store and also SteamSpy APIs. Steam gave information about games available on its platform, while SteamSpy gave estimated ownership and other game statistics. This dataset is available for public and can be shared rather than an official government or academic research dataset. I did not find anything about specific research grant or government mandate for this one too

**Original Dataset Purpose.** The dataset was created to give info about games that are on Steam for data analysis and research. It has information such as game genres, prices, reviews, estimated ownership, and average playtime. These variables are important to my project because they can help me find factors that help in making video game popular and successful.

**Collection method.** The data was collected automatically from Steam and SteamSpy using computer programs. Information from these sources was then added into CSV files. This is secondary data collected from online gaming platforms.

**Coverage and resolution.** The dataset has about 27,000 games available on Steam. The data was collected around May 2019. Each row in the main steam.csv file is one game on steam. The dataset includes game titles, release dates, genres, prices, categories, estimated owners, ratings, and playtime. but it is only limited to PC games that are on Steam and does not represent the entire video game industry.

**Licence.** The license for this dataset is the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence. This allows reuse with appropriate attribution, As long as the licence rules are followed.

**Access.** The dataset is publicly available on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nikdavis/steam-store-games. It can be downloaded as a ZIP file containing many CSV files, including steam.csv, which I plan to use for my analysis. Other researchers can access the dataset through the same page.

**Known problems.** One of the limitation is that the dataset was collected in 2019, so it does not include very new games or reflect current prices, reviews, and player activity. The ownership figures are estimates rather than verified sales numbers. The dataset are only about Steam games(pc), that mean it may not apply to console games or other platform games. I will also check for missing values, duplicates, and inconsistencies before beginning my analysis.

```{r source-2-load}
raw_2 <- read_csv("data/raw/steam.csv") 
glimpse(raw_2) |> select(1:6)

```

## 2.3: Investigated and rejected sources

Essential Facts About the U.S. Video Game Industry (2026) — Entertainment Software Association (ESA).
I considered this report because i wanted to also find correlation between age of gamers, what they play and see if there is correlation between age and game sales. However, it mainly provides combined or summarized statistics from many individual observations rather than player-age information for individual games, making it difficult to connect age demographics with game sales and success.

## 2.4: What I could not find

As i mentioned above,I initially wanted to explore whether the average age of video game players has a relationship with game success. But, I could not find a freely accessible dataset that provides player-age demographics for individual games with their sales or popularity.
i found some related information, but the available information I found was either already analyzed into graph ,etc or did not include the detailed data I needed. Because of this, I decided not to include player age in my analysis and will instead focus on factors such as genre, platform, release year, ratings, and sales.

I will not also combine and republish the datasets as a new downloadable dataset unless i find out that i have permission to do that.

# 4: Consent and identifiability

 My data is not describing people because it is about sales, game ratings, genre, and other stuff do not describe people (eg name, date of birth, etc).Since I am not collecting personal information or doing surveys or interviews, individual participant consent is not needed for my analysis.

**Consent.** 
I did not collect the data myself. Both datasets were collected by other people from  VGChartz, Metacritic, Steam, and SteamSpy. The datasets contain information about video games rather than individual players. I could not confirm what users were told when their ratings or reviews were originally collected. However, I will only use the available game level information for my analysis and will not try to identify individual users.

**Identifiability.**
None of the dataset contains individual player names, usernames, addresses, or other direct personal information. Each observation represents a video game or a game on a particular platform rather than an individual player. Although the datasets include user ratings and estimated player ownership, these are reported as combined information from many players rather than identifiable player records. Therefore, the risk of identifying individual players from the data is low.

**How sensitive data will be used.** 
i dont think the project i am trying to do is gonna have sensitive information because of how my project is and the data i am gonna be using are not personal or sensitive.  I do not expect to need anonymization or suppression of personal identifiers because none are included in the variables I plan to analyze.

# 5: Exclusions and harms

## 5.1: Excluded data from the audit

At this stage, I have not removed any columns or rows from the datasets because I am still looking through the data. However, I may exclude records with missing information, especially missing sales figures or review scores, depending on the analysis. Removing these records could affect my results because some games or platforms may be less represented than others. I will document any changes I make during data cleaning.

## 5.2: Who could be harmed
people that can be harmed are game developers, publishers, and smaller gaming companies. They could be negatively affected if my findings are misunderstood or misused. For example, maybe if my analysis suggests that certain genres or types of games are less successful, people might assume that games in those categories are not worth developing or investing in. This could discourage some smaller developers who create games for those audiences. Also, the datasets contain estimated sales and ownership figures, so treating these estimates as exact numbers could lead to unfair comparisons.s

## 5.3: Unreleased working data
I would not publicly share the original Video Game Sales with Ratings dataset because its licence is unknown. However, I can provide a link to the original Kaggle page so others can access it themselves. I plan to share my analysis and R code while giving credit to the original data sources.
